title_en: Re-run: Midnight Madness: Ryan Patch and Jon Seale
title_zh: 重播：午夜疯狂（Midnight Madness）：Ryan Patch 与 Jon Seale
subtitle_zh: 《Money Stuff》主播 Matt Levine 与 Katie Greifeld 对话 Gotham Immersive（Great Gotham Challenge）联合创始人 Ryan Patch 和 Jon Seale，揭秘华尔街通宵慈善谜题寻宝 Midnight Madness 的幕后设计。
description: Re-run: Midnight Madness: Ryan Patch and Jon Seale

speakers.1: Ryan Patch（Gotham Immersive / Great Gotham Challenge 联合创始人，谜题寻宝设计师）
speakers.2: Matt Levine（彭博观点专栏作家，《Money Stuff》主播）
speakers.3: Jon Seale（Gotham Immersive / Great Gotham Challenge 联合创始人，谜题寻宝设计师）
speakers.4: Katie Greifeld（彭博记者、《Open Interest》主播，本期《Money Stuff》联合主持）

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: 彭博音频工作室（Bloomberg Audio Studios）。

turns.en: Podcasts. Radio.
turns.zh: 播客。电台。

turns.en: News.
turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to the Money Stuff Podcast. This week we have a rerun of an interview that we first aired back in May 2025. It's a conversation that Katie and I had with Ryan Patch and John Seale, the guys who run Midnight Madness, the huge overnight puzzle hunt across New York City. Midnight Madness is happening again in just a couple of weeks on October 10th, So we thought it was a perfect time to revisit this conversation. Enjoy. I feel like it's going to be weird to do an intro, but like, it's the Money Stuff Podcast. We're here today with, I think, our second episode with a guest.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎来到《Money Stuff》播客。本周我们重播一期最早在 2025 年 5 月播出的访谈。这是我和 Katie 与 Ryan Patch、John Seale 的对话——他们俩操办着 Midnight Madness，也就是那场横跨整个纽约市、通宵进行的大型谜题寻宝（puzzle hunt）。Midnight Madness 再过几周、也就是 10 月 10 日又要开跑了，所以我们觉得现在正是重温这段对话的绝佳时机。请享用。感觉做这个开场会有点怪，但毕竟这是《Money Stuff》播客嘛。今天请到的，我想是我们第二期有嘉宾参与的节目。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: With two guests.
turns.zh: 而且是两位嘉宾。

turns.en: Our second and third guests.
turns.zh: 是我们的第二位和第三位嘉宾。

turns.en: Second and third guests. They are Ryan Patch and John Seale of the Great Gotham Challenge, two creators of puzzle hunts.
turns.zh: 第二位和第三位嘉宾。他们是来自 Great Gotham Challenge 的 Ryan Patch 和 John Seale，两位谜题寻宝的设计者。

turns.en: Welcome.
turns.zh: 欢迎。

turns.en: Welcome.
turns.zh: 欢迎。

turns.en: That's about all you need to say. We make puzzle hunts.
turns.zh: 介绍到这儿差不多就够了。我们就是做谜题寻宝的。

turns.en: We got in touch because I am a degenerate puzzle hunter in my way. And Ryan and John are taking over or sort of have taken over the big financial industry puzzle hunt that I have done occasionally, which is sometimes called Compass, but is mostly called Midnight Madness and runs overnight this year in October. So welcome, John and Ryan. Thank you. Happy to be here.
turns.zh: 我们之所以联系上，是因为我自己也算个走火入魔的谜题寻宝玩家。Ryan 和 John 正在接手——或者说已经接手了——那场金融圈的大型谜题寻宝，我偶尔也参加过，它有时叫 Compass，但更多时候叫 Midnight Madness，今年 10 月通宵开跑。所以欢迎，John 和 Ryan。谢谢，很高兴来到这儿。

turns.en: Coming soon to New York City street near you.
turns.zh: 即将登陆你家门口的纽约街头。

turns.en: This is a podcast probably about money, stuff related to money.
turns.zh: 这是一档大概跟钱有关、跟钱相关的事情有关的播客。

turns.en: That's what we bill it as.
turns.zh: 我们就是这么宣传的。

turns.en: It's not always true, but that's kind of what we say. And it has a listenership that includes a lot of financial industry and tech industry people. And the overlap of that audience with people who do puzzle hunts is meaningful, but it's not perfect. by any stretch of the imagination. And so I kind of want to explain what a puzzle hunt is. And I feel like you guys might say that you're something other than puzzle hunt guys exactly, but I really want to explain what puzzles are. So can I prompt you with that?
turns.zh: 这话也不总是真的，但我们大概就这么说。我们的听众里有不少金融圈和科技圈的人。而这批听众跟玩谜题寻宝的人之间是有交集的，交集还不小，但也绝非完美重合——差得远呢。所以我想解释一下什么是谜题寻宝。我猜你们俩可能会说，自己并不完全是『谜题寻宝 guy』那一挂的，但我真的很想解释清楚谜题到底是什么。那我能就此给你们抛个话头吗？

turns.en: I think sometime in the 90s, maybe before the MIT Mystery Hunt started, I got the sense that that is the beginning of the industry that we are weirdly a part of, largely by accident, I would say. because when Ryan and I decided to start designing puzzle hunts, we weren't aware of any of the existing ones. We thought we were making something that no one had ever heard of before. A puzzle hunt, in definition, doesn't have to be location-based, but in our case and in many cases, it's a location-based hunt in which people travel from place to place, solve a complex puzzle, and by puzzle, I don't mean jigsaw puzzle, but they receive a series of clues and pieces of information that that have to be combined in some way and thought of laterally in order to yield a solution. And that solution will often take them to a new place and they'll kind of repeat that process. Maybe people are familiar with the amazing race. It's combining elements of something like the amazing race with elements of an escape room and all into a competition in which people are competing against each other Most of the time in small teams to prove their mettle and arrive at the end first or with the highest standing that they can.
turns.zh: 我觉得大概是 90 年代某个时候，也许在 MIT 神秘寻宝（MIT Mystery Hunt）开始之前——我有种感觉，那就是我们这个行业的起点，而我们稀里古怪地成了其中一员，而且我得说，多半是误打误撞。因为当初 Ryan 和我决定开始设计谜题寻宝时，我们对现存的那些一无所知，还以为自己在创造一个从没人听说过的东西。就定义而言，谜题寻宝不一定非得基于地点，但在我们这里、以及很多情况下，它是一种基于地点的寻宝：人们从一个地方跑到另一个地方，解开一个复杂的谜题——我说的谜题不是拼图（jigsaw puzzle），而是他们会拿到一系列线索和信息碎片，必须以某种方式把它们组合起来、进行横向思维（lateral thinking），才能得出答案。而这个答案往往又会把他们带到新的地方，如此循环往复。也许有人熟悉《极速前进》（The Amazing Race）。它就是把类似《极速前进》的元素和密室逃脱（escape room）的元素融合到一起，变成一场竞赛：人们相互比拼，通常是以小队形式，来证明自己的本事，力争第一个到达终点，或者拿到尽可能高的名次。

turns.en: I became aware of puzzle hunts before I became aware of escape rooms. And I don't know if that's like the actual chronology in the world where like people invent.
turns.zh: 我接触到谜题寻宝，是在知道密室逃脱之前。我不确定这在现实世界里、在『东西被发明出来』的时间线上是不是也这样。

turns.en: It's not my experience.
turns.zh: 反正跟我的经历不一样。

turns.en: Yeah. Well, puzzle hunts are pretty niche.
turns.zh: 是啊。嗯，谜题寻宝还是挺小众的。

turns.en: Yeah, escape rooms came after puzzle hunts.
turns.zh: 对，密室逃脱是在谜题寻宝之后才出现的。

turns.en: Yeah, that's what I thought. They sort of grew out of the puzzle hunt idea and you could put an escape room in a place and sell it to people every day rather than do it once a year.
turns.zh: 嗯，我也这么想。密室逃脱算是从谜题寻宝的点子长出来的，你可以把一间密室固定开在某个地方，天天卖票给人玩，而不是一年才搞一次。

turns.en: And escape rooms are definitely a little more consumer-oriented, whereas a puzzle hunt, you have to be a certain glutton for punishment or at least intellectual stimuli. Escape rooms are great because you know at the end of 60 minutes you're done, whereas a puzzle hunt, if you fail, you're floundering in the middle of some urban landscape trying to figure out where to go next.
turns.zh: 而且密室逃脱肯定更偏向大众消费，而谜题寻宝嘛，你得是那种有点自虐倾向、或者至少是对智力刺激上瘾的人。密室逃脱的好处在于，你知道 60 分钟一到就结束了；而谜题寻宝要是你卡了壳，就会在某片城市景观的正中央手忙脚乱，完全不知道该往哪儿走。

turns.en: At 3 a.m.
turns.zh: 而且是在凌晨三点。

turns.en: Often.
turns.zh: 经常如此。

turns.en: But you know what I would say is that I think escape rooms and puzzle hunts share an origin story, I would guess, which is that it's people saying, what if we could be in a video game in real life? So it's kind of taking this idea of a quest and something to be solved and creating a real life experience around that.
turns.zh: 不过我会这么说：我猜密室逃脱和谜题寻宝有着共同的起源故事，那就是有人在想——要是我们能在现实生活里进入一款电子游戏，那会怎样？所以这基本上就是把『任务』和『待解之谜』这个点子拿来，围绕它打造出一段现实生活中的体验。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: What differentiates a puzzle hunt from a scavenger hunt? Or is that just a meaningless distinction?
turns.zh: 谜题寻宝和寻物游戏（scavenger hunt）的区别在哪儿？还是说这区分根本没有意义？

turns.en: Is it the puzzles?
turns.zh: 是因为谜题吗？

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.en: You get clues and you have to think critically in scavenger hunts.
turns.zh: 可在寻物游戏里你也要拿线索、也要动脑做批判性思考啊。

turns.en: There's definitely a blurry line between the two. But I think that the puzzle hunts are often once you arrive at a location, you're not just there to find something. You're there to solve a complex situation. And there's pen and paper puzzle hunts. where you just like go to a location and you're given a few pieces of paper and they're all kind of these very crosswordy or language-based or math-based puzzles that you wind up solving. And then they result to a keyword or often the next location that you're going to. And then you go to the next location, you get handed another set of papers. So there's always some very specific activity. Now, we came kind of this from more of the immersion angle. We kind of asked ourselves the question, what would it look like if people felt like they were in a movie? And then we started creating these quests and then we realized, well, to kind of unlock the door that kind of lets you into the next thing, there needs to be a puzzle. And so we kind of came at it from a little more of a, an angle saying, well, we need to have a key for that door. We need to have a password for that door and started slowly integrating puzzles. So we kind of backed into the puzzle hunt community from more of like an immersive angle. Whereas the puzzle hunt community has then kind of been pulled a little more into the immersive community through escape rooms, through immersive theater. And then you have, yeah, the scavenger hunt community, which is kind of geocaching adjacent and just making hunts for your 10-year-old kids adjacent. The worst version of a scavenger hunt is like, take pictures of five out of state license plates or like, you know, get a photo of a person with a beard and is kind of our guiding light that we move away from.
turns.zh: 这两者之间确实界线模糊。但我觉得谜题寻宝往往是：你到了一个地点，不只是去找某样东西，而是要去解开一个复杂的局面。还有那种纸笔谜题寻宝（pen and paper puzzle hunt）——你去到一个地点，人家给你几张纸，上面全是很像填字游戏那种、或者基于语言、基于数学的谜题，你最后把它们解出来，然后得到一个关键词，或者往往就是你接下来要去的下一个地点。你到了下一个地点，又有人递给你另一叠纸。所以总是有某种非常具体的活动。而我们入行，更多是从沉浸感（immersion）的角度切入的。我们当时问自己：如果人们觉得自己置身于一部电影里，那会是什么样子？于是我们开始设计这些任务，然后意识到，嗯，要打开那扇通往下一关的门，就得有一道谜题。所以我们的切入角度更像是：我们需要给那扇门配一把钥匙、设一个密码，然后开始慢慢把谜题整合进去。所以我们算是从沉浸式的那个方向，倒着摸进了谜题寻宝这个圈子。而谜题寻宝圈子后来又被更多地拉进了沉浸式圈子——通过密室逃脱、通过沉浸式戏剧。然后呢，你还有寻物游戏那个圈子，它跟地理藏宝（geocaching）沾亲带故，也跟『给你家十岁小孩设计个寻宝游戏』沾亲带故。寻物游戏最糟糕的版本就是那种『拍下五块外州车牌』，或者『跟一个留胡子的人合个影』——而这恰恰是我们避之唯恐不及的反面灯塔。

turns.en: We draw a distinction in our world between puzzles and tasks. And a puzzle is, it requires some sort of lateral thinking and a task is just an action that you complete. So I think a lot of scavenger hunts are task-based versus a puzzle requires you to use your brain in a different way.
turns.zh: 在我们这行里，我们会区分『谜题』和『任务』。谜题需要某种横向思维，而任务只是一个你去完成的动作。所以我觉得很多寻物游戏是基于任务的，而谜题则要求你用一种不同的方式动脑。

turns.en: Do you have like a classic puzzle or like a, form of puzzle or a way to describe more concretely what the puzzles and puzzle hunts are? Because like to me, and I have not, I don't think done your challenges, although I think I did at Midnight Matter, a compass that might've been partly you're doing. And I have a sense, like an inarticulate sense of what puzzle hunt puzzles feel like. You know, I've done, I don't know, four or five puzzle hunts in an escape room or two, but like, how do you think about puzzles and like, what is a puzzle and like, what kinds of things are puzzles? Could you give a puzzle that we could talk about on a podcast? Sure.
turns.zh: 你们有没有那种经典的谜题，或者某种谜题的形式，能更具体地描述一下谜题寻宝里的谜题到底是什么？因为对我来说——我大概没玩过你们设计的挑战，虽然我觉得我在 Midnight Madness、在某场 Compass 里玩过，那场可能有你们参与。我对谜题寻宝的谜题是什么感觉，有一种说不清道不明的感觉。你懂的，我玩过四五场谜题寻宝、一两间密室，但你们是怎么思考谜题的？什么才算一道谜题？哪些东西算谜题？能不能给我们举一个可以在播客里聊的谜题？当然可以。

turns.en: I think every puzzle hunt has its own tradition of how it defines a puzzle. And Ryan and I are the first people to be in charge of the Midnight Madness tradition, kind of coming from the outside, not having played and not being from the finance industry. So we had to do our homework and spend a lot of time learning what's a puzzle by the definition of Midnight Madness. And one thing that we identified is Each one should involve a logical leap. So there's typically a mental connection that you make between two different types of information. So an example of a puzzle that I think is a good illustration of this from an event that we did a few years ago was designed by our friend Josh Stabiner. And it's a puzzle in which you receive a rap sheet that looks like a police description of several perpetrators of criminals. And each one has a description and then a picture of what looks like a fingerprint for each one. But you use clues in the descriptions and you use clues of what the visual of the fingerprint looks like to actually make a connection that you're not looking at fingerprints, you're looking at topographical maps of mountains. And each one you discover as you kind of read through the text and look for words that might seem out of place and kind of, evidence that the descriptions are not quite fitting well to like how a policeman might describe a criminal to recognize that each of the seven is representing the seven highest peaks on each continent. And so then you use that information to go back to the first descriptions. And in there, you work with the information you have to yield a final solution, which is a key word. But in order to do that, you have to be able to make this mental leap. and recognize that one thing is actually representing another.
turns.zh: 我觉得每一场谜题寻宝都有它自己定义『谜题』的传统。而 Ryan 和我，是第一批从外部接手 Midnight Madness 这套传统来负责它的人——我们没玩过它，也不是金融圈出身。所以我们得做功课，花很多时间去搞明白：按 Midnight Madness 的定义，什么才算一道谜题。我们识别出的一点是：每道谜题都应该包含一次逻辑跳跃（logical leap）。也就是说，你通常要在两种不同类型的信息之间建立一种思维上的关联。举个例子，有一道谜题我觉得很好地说明了这一点，它出自我们几年前办的一场活动，由我们的朋友 Josh Stabiner 设计。这道谜题里，你会拿到一份看起来像警方对几名罪犯嫌犯描述的案件卷宗（rap sheet）。每个人有一段描述，然后配一张看起来像指纹的图。但你要利用描述里的线索，以及那张『指纹』图像上的线索，去建立一个关联：你看到的其实不是指纹，而是山峰的等高线地形图（topographical maps）。当你通读文字、寻找那些显得格格不入的词、寻找那些说明『这段描述跟警察描述罪犯的口吻不太对得上』的证据时，你会逐一发现——这七个，每一个代表的其实是各大洲的最高峰（seven highest peaks）。于是你再用这个信息回到最初那些描述里去，用手上的信息推导出最终答案，也就是一个关键词。但要做到这一点，你必须能完成这次思维上的跳跃，意识到一样东西其实是在代表另一样东西。

turns.en: How do you make them difficult without being infuriating? Because this is something different, but Bloomberg has a weekly quiz.
turns.zh: 你们怎么把谜题设计得够难、又不至于把人逼疯？因为这其实是另一码事，但彭博有个每周小测验（weekly quiz）。

turns.en: Quiz go.
turns.zh: 小测验，走起。

turns.en: Matt, you've played it.
turns.zh: Matt，你玩过的。

turns.en: I have. You've written it, right?
turns.zh: 玩过。是你出的题，对吧？

turns.en: I used to be the curator of the quiz, and one of the metrics on which I judged myself was by how many people who started the quiz completed the quiz. And there was like this fine balance I had to find between making it challenging but not making it annoying. So how do you find that balance when you're putting together puzzles and make sure that people basically don't rage quit?
turns.zh: 我以前是这个测验的策划人（curator），而我给自己打分的一个指标，就是有多少人开始了测验、又有多少人把它做完了。我必须在『够有挑战性』和『别惹人烦』之间找到那个微妙的平衡。那你们在设计谜题时，是怎么找到这个平衡、确保大家不至于愤而退出（rage quit）的？

turns.en: Yes, you're our sister in pain, I see.
turns.zh: 看来你是我们同病相怜的姐妹啊。

turns.en: I think that's the number one skill of a good puzzle creator. I think that right there is the magic sauce is figuring out something that's just hard enough that makes people really feel like they've gone on a journey and they were just about to quit, but then they had that spark of inspiration that turned it all around for them. And then everything fell into place. And then looking back on it, it's like, oh, of course that was the answer. It could never have not been the answer. And bringing people on that journey and allowing them to go on that journey themselves. And then by the end of it, having that, I heard it recently described as I think secondhand fun or second degree fun, where it's like, it's sucked in the moment, but when you look back on it, it's a pleasureful thing. And so creating that moment, it's very difficult and we've struggled with it. And, you know, we created the great Gotham challenge. I created the first one by myself. John was a participant. This is how we started working together. And no one finished it. Everyone rage quit. It was in 2009. The stock market had crashed. I just graduated college and couldn't get a job. And so me and another friend created this and it was supposed to be like a four hour thing. Everyone just texted us after hour four and was like, I am a quarter of the way through. Please put a bullet in my head. And so it's just like, okay, come to the finish line. But anyways, we've gotten better. We've been doing this for about 11 years and a lot of it is playtesting. Like we have a community of people that just playtest our puzzles and They time themselves and we make sure we know how long a puzzle should take and what the right deviation is. And it's also a lot of argument. Like we've just got people that we really trust and who have done a lot of these things. And someone says, this is way too hard. This is way too easy. And we just go 12 rounds until we find something that we all agree on. And we trust each other. So part of it's not working in a vacuum and part of it's just a lot of experience and a part of it's playtesting. John and I are creative by nature, and we brought in an operations person to help run our company named Teresa, who's brilliant and has saved our company many times. But one of the things she instigated is, no, we playtest things. We playtest things thoroughly.
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是优秀谜题设计者的头号技能。这就是那味『魔法酱汁』（magic sauce）——设计出一个难度恰到好处的东西，让人真的觉得自己经历了一段旅程：他们本来都要放弃了，结果灵光一闪，局面瞬间翻盘，然后一切都各就各位。回过头去看，就会觉得：哦，答案当然是它，它怎么可能是别的答案呢。带着人们踏上这段旅程、让他们自己走完这段旅程，到最后收获那种——我最近听到有人把它形容成『二手乐趣』（secondhand fun）或者『二度乐趣』（second degree fun）——就是当下痛苦得要命，可等你回头看，却是一段愉悦的经历。所以要制造出那个时刻，非常难，我们也一直在为此挣扎。你知道，我们创造了 Great Gotham Challenge。第一届是我一个人做的，John 是参与者。我们就是这么开始合作的。结果没有一个人通关，所有人都愤而退出。那是 2009 年，股市刚崩盘，我刚大学毕业、找不到工作。于是我和另一个朋友搞了这个，本来设计成大概四个小时的活动。结果四个小时一到，所有人都给我们发短信说：『我才走完四分之一，求你朝我脑袋开一枪吧。』我们就只能说：『好吧，那就走到终点线这儿来。』不管怎样，我们后来进步了。我们干这行大概 11 年了，其中很大一部分靠的是试玩测试（playtesting）。我们有一个专门帮我们试玩谜题的社群，他们会给自己计时，我们借此确保知道一道谜题应该花多长时间、合理的误差范围是多少。这里面也有很多争论。我们有一批非常信任、又做过很多这类东西的人，有人说『这个太难了』，有人说『这个太简单了』，我们就来回吵上十二个回合，直到找到一个大家都认可的方案。我们彼此信任。所以一部分在于别闭门造车，一部分在于丰富的经验，还有一部分在于试玩测试。John 和我天生是搞创意的，于是我们请来一位运营的人帮我们打理公司，她叫 Teresa，非常厉害，好几次把公司从危难中救了出来。她推动的一件事就是：不行，我们必须做试玩测试，而且要彻底地测。

turns.en: I think another part of the answer to Katie's question is when I've done puzzle hunts, there's some sort of hint mechanism where you can, without fully giving up, you can give up a little and get some sort of help. Can you talk about how you think about that?
turns.zh: 我觉得 Katie 这个问题的答案还有一部分是：我玩谜题寻宝时，总会有某种提示机制，让你不用完全认输，也能稍微『认一点点输』、得到一些帮助。你们能谈谈是怎么设计这个的吗？

turns.en: Yeah. And it's interesting because we've seen this done different ways. And in the Midnight Madness puzzle hunt that we stage every other year for the finance industry, there's kind of a bespoke, personalized, what's called game controller who meters out hints.
turns.zh: 嗯。有意思的是，我们见过各种不同的做法。在我们每隔一年为金融圈举办的那场 Midnight Madness 谜题寻宝里，会有一种量身定制、个性化的角色，叫『游戏操控者』（game controller），由他来一点点发放提示。

turns.en: It's like your personal tormentor. Right. Right. Exactly.
turns.zh: 就像你的专属折磨者。对吧。对对。没错。

turns.en: And this is actually something very unique about the Wall Street vibe is that the game controllers are known to be a little malicious and a little kind of Because we've been kind of apprenticing with the current creators for the last four years and we've taken it over this year. And so we've watched them and tried to learn and we've been like, this seems weird. This seems mean. And they're like, oh no, it's what people want. Like it's what the, it's what the players want. That's done in a very like bespoke, handcrafted concierge way, both the hinting and the tormenting. Whereas like on our Great Gotham Challenge branded puzzle hunts that we do, there's kind of a unified pre-canned hint system that That, you know, when you feel like you're at a dead end, you can take a hint and there's a certain time penalty. And we've introduced a fun gamified mechanic where the longer you're on a puzzle, the less penalty time you get. And so, yeah, there absolutely needs to be a hint system. And that's absolutely a way that you keep people within the same universe. If there was no hint system, then you'd see deviations of 200% on times.
turns.zh: 而这其实正是华尔街范儿特别独特的地方——那些游戏操控者是出了名的有点坏心眼、有点那么……过去四年我们一直像是给现任设计者当学徒，今年正式接了过来。我们一直观察他们、努力学，心里想着：这看起来好奇怪，这也太刻薄了吧。他们却说：不不，这正是大家想要的，是玩家们想要的。无论是给提示还是折磨人，都是以一种非常量身定制、手工打造、管家式（concierge）的方式进行的。而在我们自己 Great Gotham Challenge 品牌的谜题寻宝里，则是一套统一的、预先设定好的提示系统：当你觉得走进死胡同时，可以领一个提示，但要付出一定的时间罚分。我们还引入了一种好玩的游戏化机制——你在某道谜题上耗得越久，领提示时的罚时就越少。所以，是的，绝对需要有一套提示系统。这也绝对是让所有人都待在同一个『宇宙』里的办法。要是没有提示系统，你就会看到用时相差 200% 的情况。

turns.en: My experience of like Compass or Midnight Madness is like, if you're like getting on the subway to go to the wrong burrow, your game control will be like, hold on. Right, yeah, yeah, yeah. There's some amount of like, don't do something really stupid.
turns.zh: 我玩 Compass 或 Midnight Madness 的体验是这样的：如果你正要上地铁、结果坐去了错误的行政区（borough），你的游戏操控者就会说：『等等。』对，是是是。总归有那么一层『别干太蠢的事』的意思。

turns.en: And that's the, yeah, that's the designer's job is to, yeah, figuring out how to let people fail enough that they go through those peaks and valleys of emotions, but not letting them fail so much that they're just destroyed.
turns.zh: 是啊，这正是设计者的工作——想办法让人们失败到足以经历那些情绪的起起落落，但又别让他们失败到彻底崩溃的地步。

turns.en: Yeah, you want to feel like you can fail so that when you succeed, you feel good about it.
turns.zh: 对，你希望能感觉到『自己是可能失败的』，这样当你成功时，才会有成就感。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: Can we talk about Midnight Madness? I've written about having done one or two compass hunts, which my understanding is that, like, at some point, a kind of Goldman Sachs-affiliated group of Wall Street people started a Midnight Madness puzzle hunt, possibly named after a movie of the same name. And... It was called Midnight Madness because it started at, I don't know, 4 p.m. and went until 2 p.m. the next day.
turns.zh: 我们能聊聊 Midnight Madness 吗？我写过自己参加过一两场 Compass 寻宝。据我了解，某个时候，一群跟高盛（Goldman Sachs）有关联的华尔街人发起了一场 Midnight Madness 谜题寻宝，名字可能是取自一部同名电影。而……它之所以叫『午夜疯狂』（Midnight Madness），是因为它下午四点开始，一直搞到第二天下午两点。

turns.en: Everything you've heard is correct, yes.
turns.zh: 你听说的都对，没错。

turns.en: Yeah. And it was run by, I think, Alicia Wiesel at Goldman. And then it became so overwhelming that my understanding was, like, the winners got to run it the next time. And I know, like, Colin Tykel ran it for a while. And that is, like, in my understanding, the premier, like, Wall Street puzzle hunt. And all of the teams are, like... Eight Goldman teams and six Chain Street teams. Is that basically correct?
turns.zh: 嗯。我记得是高盛的 Alicia Wiesel 在操办。后来这事变得太繁重，据我了解，就变成了由上一届的赢家来办下一届。我还知道 Colin Tykel 办过一阵子。在我理解里，这就是华尔街首屈一指的谜题寻宝。所有队伍都是……八支高盛队、六支其他华尔街机构的队。这说法基本对吗？

turns.en: Most of that's correct. Alicia designed it for, I think, maybe a decade or a little less. And at some point, I think he decided it was too much for him to continue and just decided, I can't keep doing this.
turns.zh: 大部分都对。Alicia 设计了它大概十年、或者不到十年。到某个时候，我想他觉得这对他来说太吃力、没法再继续下去了，就决定：『我不能再干这个了。』

turns.en: I need to quit.
turns.zh: 我得退出了。

turns.en: And the team that won the year that he called his final year decided that they loved the game too much to let it die. So they said, we'll take over. We'll Put it under a different name so that people recognize that it's under new management. They ran it for several years and then they decided we can't keep doing this. It's destroying our lives and our relationships.
turns.zh: 而在他所谓『最后一届』那年夺冠的那支队伍，觉得太爱这个游戏、不忍心让它消亡，于是说：『我们来接手。我们会换一个名字，让大家知道它已经换人管理了。』他们办了好几年，然后也决定：『我们不能再干下去了，这正在毁掉我们的生活和感情。』

turns.en: Because all these people have like real jobs in the financial industry and also extracurricularly design these insane things. All night puzzle hunts.
turns.zh: 因为这些人在金融圈都有正经的本职工作，却还要在业余设计出这些疯狂的东西——通宵的谜题寻宝。

turns.en: As opposed to us who have fake jobs in the financial industry. Yes, that's correct. No, we have real jobs in puzzle hunts.
turns.zh: 不像我们，在金融圈干的是『假工作』。是的，没错。不，我们在谜题寻宝这行干的是真工作。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So this is your job. It's not their job.
turns.zh: 对，正是。所以这是你们的工作，不是他们的工作。

turns.en: It's a little more sustainable for us. But yes, exactly. Like, I don't know how they could possibly do it because this is my full time job. It already is so hard for me. I can't imagine working at a hedge fund while simultaneously doing this.
turns.zh: 对我们来说更可持续一点。但是的，正是如此。我真不知道他们怎么可能做得到，因为这是我的全职工作，对我来说已经够难了。我无法想象一边在对冲基金上班、一边还搞这个。

turns.en: So you guys are professional puzzle hunt makers and they are professional hedge fund managers. As you look at their work, what do you think? Were they good at it? If you have like the regular puzzle hunt community and then you have like the hedge fund guys, is there a different style or mindset?
turns.zh: 所以你们是职业谜题寻宝制作者，而他们是职业对冲基金经理。看着他们做的东西，你们怎么想？他们擅长吗？如果把常规的谜题寻宝社群和对冲基金那帮人放一起比，风格或思维方式会有不同吗？

turns.en: Yeah, that's something Ryan and I were just discussing, actually. There are things that are unique to it. There are ways that maybe we look at things a bit differently. For instance, talking about hints, Ryan and I, as puzzle designers, we kind of believe that a really well-designed puzzle should be able to be completed by a good puzzler without needing to be hinted in any way. Whereas I think they're coming from a world in which they feel like if it's not hard enough to require someone to take hints, then it's not hard enough. So that's been an adjustment, I think, for us to kind of recognize.
turns.zh: 是啊，其实这正是 Ryan 和我刚才在讨论的。这里面有些东西是它独有的，有些方面我们看问题的角度可能不太一样。比方说提示这块，作为谜题设计者，Ryan 和我大致相信：一道真正设计得好的谜题，一个厉害的解谜者应该能在完全不需要任何提示的情况下解出来。而我觉得他们来自另一个世界，在他们看来，如果一道谜题没难到需要人去领提示，那它就还不够难。所以这对我们来说，是一种需要慢慢认识、适应的差异。

turns.en: We're a little more breadcrumb that leap of logic in a way that like at the end of a good murder mystery, you look back and you're like, oh, the hints were always there that it was the butler. And so we're a little more on that end versus, yeah, they're more like, you have to make this leap of logic with no prior breadcrumbs.
turns.zh: 我们更偏向于给那次逻辑跳跃撒『面包屑』（线索）——就像一部好的推理悬疑剧看到结尾，你回头一想：哦，『凶手是管家』的线索一直都在。所以我们更偏向那一端；而他们更像是：你必须完成这次逻辑跳跃，且事先没有任何面包屑可循。

turns.en: I'm with you. I've had some Midnight Madness experiences where you're like, you get the hint and you're like, no one would have gotten that. That makes no sense. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我站你们这边。我有过几次 Midnight Madness 的经历：你拿到提示后心想，这玩意儿没人猜得出来啊，完全说不通。是的。

turns.en: Another big distinction, though, that we've come to terms with, though, that I think is really interesting and says a lot, and we didn't believe this to be true when we started, but I think we've come around to the idea that the people who are attracted to this Midnight Madness game who come from Wall Street, they do crave, I hesitate to use the word glutton for punishment, but they do crave a certain amount of intensity and some would even say torture that I think was surprising to us.
turns.zh: 不过还有一个我们逐渐接受了的大区别，我觉得很有意思、也很能说明问题。刚入行时我们并不相信这是真的，但后来我们慢慢认同了这个看法：那些被 Midnight Madness 吸引、来自华尔街的人，他们确实渴望——我有点不想用『自虐狂』（glutton for punishment）这个词——但他们确实渴望某种强度，有人甚至会说渴望某种『折磨』，这一点当初让我们很意外。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, just the fact that it is sort of runs overnight is cruel.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，光是它通宵进行这一点，就已经够残忍了。

turns.en: In a way, it's like endurance athletics, but with your mind and your body.
turns.zh: 从某种意义上说，这就像耐力运动，只不过是同时考验你的头脑和身体。

turns.en: Totally. Yeah. You have a day job running puzzle hunts under your own brand and like puzzle hunt activities for corporate clients.
turns.zh: 完全同意。是的。你们有一份正职，就是以自有品牌运营谜题寻宝，以及为企业客户设计谜题寻宝活动。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: My sense is that a lot of your clients are also in the financial industry and like puzzle hunting and finance overlap a lot. Is that right?
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，你们的很多客户也在金融行业，而且谜题寻宝和金融圈重合度很高。对吗？

turns.en: Yes. You're onto us. We didn't mean to do it that way, but the market found us. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，被你看穿了。我们本来没打算走这条路，但市场自己找上了我们。嗯。

turns.en: What do you think it is about like financial people and puzzle hunts? Like where do they go together?
turns.zh: 你们觉得金融人和谜题寻宝之间，到底是哪里对上了？它们是怎么凑到一块儿的？

turns.en: Several things. One is I think the finance industry and the tech industry have become really closely intertwined. And as I said, the tradition of the MIT mystery hunt, a lot of these people that come from Cambridge end up in New York, end up doing finance related jobs. And so they've crafted a taste for this type of thing already earlier in life.
turns.zh: 有好几点。其一，我觉得金融行业和科技行业已经变得高度交织。而且就像我说的，因为 MIT 神秘寻宝的传统，很多从剑桥（Cambridge）出来的人最后到了纽约，做起了跟金融相关的工作。所以他们早在人生更早的阶段，就培养出了对这类东西的品味。

turns.en: Does everyone at MIT do the mystery hunt?
turns.zh: MIT 是不是每个人都玩神秘寻宝？

turns.en: I don't think everyone does it. And a lot of people who do it are also not currently at MIT.
turns.zh: 我不觉得每个人都玩。而且很多玩这个的人，眼下也并不在 MIT。

turns.en: I've been invited on teams that it seemed like more trouble than I was worth. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我被人邀请加入过一些队伍，感觉我带来的麻烦比我这个人还值。是啊。

turns.en: I mean, that's a, that's like a three day event or a four day event.
turns.zh: 我是说，那可是个三天或四天的活动。

turns.en: And it seems like a hundred people and you can do it remotely. It just seems like a lot.
turns.zh: 而且好像有一百人参与，还能远程玩。就是感觉工程量很大。

turns.en: It is a lot.
turns.zh: 确实很大。

turns.en: You're not wrong about that.
turns.zh: 你这话没说错。

turns.en: Our COO, Teresa participated this last year and had a fantastic time and We're going to try to go next year. And she went there on a team and it's like, how fun can like being holed up in a, in a hotel room solving puzzles, you know, but it really seems like the winning teams are, it's not just about puzzle solving acumen, but about organization of brainpower. You know, how do you effectively deploy a hundred people to effectively manage problems and contribute and make these lateral leaps and, It seems like that's the key to the MIT mystery hunt, which is, I think, such an interesting social management problem.
turns.zh: 我们的首席运营官（COO）Teresa 去年参加了，玩得很开心，明年我们也打算去。她是加入一支队伍去的。你想想，一群人窝在酒店房间里解谜题，能有多好玩？但看起来，获胜的队伍靠的不只是解谜的敏锐度，而是对『脑力』的组织调度。你知道，怎么才能有效地部署一百个人，去高效地管理问题、做出贡献、完成那些横向跳跃。这似乎才是 MIT 神秘寻宝的关键——我觉得这是一个非常有意思的社会管理难题。

turns.en: Yeah, I was reading a Quartz article from 2013, I think it was, because Midnight Madness went on a bit of a hiatus and then it came back.
turns.zh: 是啊，我在读一篇《石英财经》（Quartz）的文章，我记得是 2013 年的，因为 Midnight Madness 曾经停办了一阵子，然后又回来了。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And the article is talking about how originally the thinking, you know, among the Goldman Sachs teams who participated was that they wanted to stack their teams with quants. They just wanted a lot of big brains. But the team that ended up winning... was a group that worked together. And I think they were client facing and they chalked their winning up to just, we know how to work together. We don't necessarily have the smartest guy in the room, but we all know how to manage together.
turns.zh: 那篇文章讲的是，最早的时候，参赛的高盛队伍的想法是：他们想在队里塞满量化分析师（quants），就是想要一堆最强大脑。但最终胜出的那支队伍……是一群懂得协作的人。我记得他们是做客户对接（client facing）的，他们把胜利归结为：『我们知道怎么一起干活。我们队里未必有全场最聪明的那个人，但我们都知道怎么协同管理。』

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And also like if it's all quants, like you want different kinds of intelligence too, like in solving the puzzles as well as in creating the puzzles. Like, you know, as I was thinking about like why the financial industry likes puzzle hunts, I mean, I was thinking like teamwork is always pretty heavily emphasized when you like interview at a financial firm and like the idea of like, Getting different types of intelligence together and trying to delegate responsibility and brainstorm together does seem useful in the job. And then it hadn't even occurred to me that the 100% MIT mystery hunt teams are an enormous management problem. But yes, if you can manage a puzzle hunt team of 100 people, that does seem useful for managing a hedge fund.
turns.zh: 而且，如果全是量化分析师，你其实也需要不同类型的才智——无论是解谜还是设计谜题都是如此。你知道，当我在想金融圈为什么喜欢谜题寻宝时，我想到：你去金融公司面试时，团队合作总是被特别强调；而把不同类型的才智聚到一起、试着分派责任、一起头脑风暴，这个理念在工作里确实有用。然后我此前根本没想到，那种百人规模的 MIT 神秘寻宝队伍是个巨大的管理难题。但没错，如果你能管好一支一百人的谜题寻宝队，那对管理一只对冲基金来说，确实很有用。

turns.en: They create custom software platforms just to manage the puzzles. It's incredible. I did want to go back to, you were correct in that Midnight Madness grew out of Goldman. And I'd say maybe still less than, I mean, maybe 40% of our teams are Goldman, 30 to 40% of our teams. So they're a huge supporter. And just to give the context for your listeners, this Midnight Madness is a charity event for Good Shepherd Services. And so the great part is instead of going to a fundraiser where you have to buy a table and sit through speeches and watch pretty picture videos, you stake a team to compete. And so I'd say, yeah, still definitely a huge, the biggest showing is from Goldman, but there's probably 15 to 20 different firms represented, everything from bigger investment banks to quant firms to really small shops. And I don't even know all the different types of shops that are represented there. And it goes from places where the CEO is leading the team and to places where the CEO is stakes the team and then like puts his best people on the team and shows up at the finish line or also places where just like they just look at it as a donation and let the people who want to show up.
turns.zh: 他们甚至会专门开发定制的软件平台来管理这些谜题，太不可思议了。我确实想回到刚才那点：你说得对，Midnight Madness 是从高盛里长出来的。我会说，也许还不到——嗯，我们队伍里大概有 40%、30% 到 40% 是高盛的。所以他们是个大金主。给你们的听众交代一下背景：这场 Midnight Madness 是为 Good Shepherd Services（好牧人服务机构）办的慈善活动。妙就妙在，你不用去参加那种得买一桌席位、坐着听完演讲、看完精美宣传片的募捐晚宴，而是赞助一支队伍去比赛。所以我会说，是的，出场阵容最大的仍然是高盛，但大概有 15 到 20 家不同的机构参与，从大型投行到量化公司、再到很小的工作室都有。我甚至都说不全那里到底有哪些类型的机构。有的地方是 CEO 亲自带队，有的地方是 CEO 出钱赞助队伍、把自己最能干的人塞进队里，然后本人到终点线露个面；还有的地方干脆把它当成一笔捐款，谁想去谁去。

turns.en: But the idea is like basically Midnight Madness is a fundraiser for Good Shepherd. The team is up to six people.
turns.zh: 所以基本上，Midnight Madness 就是为 Good Shepherd 办的一场募捐。每支队伍最多六个人。

turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: And it costs something like $ 40, 000 to sponsor a team. So it's exactly it's a meaningful donation. Yeah.
turns.zh: 赞助一支队伍大概要花 4 万美元。所以这确实是一笔有意义的捐款。嗯。

turns.en: And so we'll have 25 teams duking it out on October 4th, the early hours of October 5th, duking it out for the title of the most, you know, most intelligent and really best.
turns.zh: 所以今年 10 月 4 日、一直到 10 月 5 日凌晨，会有 25 支队伍一决高下，争夺那个『最聪明、最厉害』的头衔。

turns.en: So in my experience, the production values for Midnight Madness are really high. Like the year I did it most recently, it ended on the Intrepid, like the aircraft carrier, solving a puzzle on a real Enigma machine. I don't know if you know this, but it's very finance industry coded. Like you're not a hedge fund unless you have a real Enigma machine somewhere. And it was like, you know, you had to like, get clues by going to like a screening of a movie on a rooftop in Brooklyn and like there was a like chessboard in the Brooklyn Museum it was like a real pretty high-end experience I'm very interested in like talking about the puzzle aspect but like as designers I feel like you're more interested in like the cool experiences side of it you talk about that.
turns.zh: 以我的经验，Midnight Madness 的制作水准非常高。比如我最近一次参加那年，结尾是在『无畏号』（Intrepid）——就是那艘航空母舰——上用一台真正的恩尼格玛密码机（Enigma machine）解谜。不知道你们了不了解，但这在金融圈是一种很『内行』的暗号：你手里要没有一台真的恩尼格玛机，就都不好意思说自己是家对冲基金。而且，你知道吗，你得去布鲁克林某个天台参加一场电影放映来获取线索，布鲁克林博物馆里还有一个棋盘……那真是一次相当高端的体验。我很有兴趣聊聊谜题这一面，但作为设计者，我觉得你们更感兴趣的其实是那种『酷炫体验』的一面，你们说说看。

turns.en: Yeah that I mean that was really intimidating and it's interesting when Ryan and I started designing games like this when we were in college just for our friends and scraping together a couple of bucks from our own pocket and trying to dream as big as we could. And only many years later, we came across an article about the tradition of Midnight Madness and learned that there was a puzzle that year where teams had controls that were actively controlling the lights on the Empire State Building and changing the colors to solve a puzzle. And we were absolutely floored by the kind of production value available to these game designers and thought like, wow, if we could just do something like that one day, that would be the biggest dream that we could dream for ourselves. And yeah, so a lot of the fee that people contribute to stake a team does go towards the production of a very fantastic and epic game. And that's part of the appeal. It is interesting for us to try to design for the man or woman who has everything, quote unquote. And if you're super wealthy and you have all these kind of opportunities and experiences available to you on a regular basis. What is impressive? What can make an impression on that type of person? I think that's part of where this tradition has come from of like, wow, it has to be bombastic and having access to landmark locations in New York City that you wouldn't normally have is a big part of it. The scale has changed a bit. I think when Alicia was designing it, maybe a much bigger portion of the fee went towards the production value of the game and We're allocating a different kind of percentage to the charity versus the.
turns.zh: 是啊，那确实挺让人望而生畏的。有意思的是，Ryan 和我刚开始设计这类游戏时还在上大学，只是为朋友们做，从自己口袋里凑出那么几块钱，然后尽可能地把梦想做大。直到很多年后，我们偶然看到一篇讲 Midnight Madness 传统的文章，才知道有一年的谜题是：各队手里有控制器，能实时操控帝国大厦（Empire State Building）的灯光、变换颜色来解谜。我们被这些游戏设计者所能调动的制作水准彻底震惊了，心想：哇，如果哪天我们也能做一件那样的事，那就是我们能给自己许下的最大的梦想了。所以，是的，大家为赞助队伍掏的那笔费用，很大一部分确实花在了打造一款极其精彩、史诗级的游戏上，这也是它的吸引力之一。对我们来说，有意思的是要设法为那种『什么都不缺』的男人或女人做设计——打个引号。如果你超级富有，日常就能享受各种各样的机会和体验，那什么东西才算震撼？什么才能给这种人留下印象？我觉得这套传统正是由此而来：哇，它必须气派非凡，而能进入纽约市那些你平时进不去的地标场所，是其中很重要的一部分。规模有所变化。我想 Alicia 当年设计时，费用里可能有更大比例是花在游戏制作上的，而我们现在给慈善和游戏制作分配的比例不太一样……

turns.en: More to the charity, to be clear.
turns.zh: 说清楚点，是给慈善的更多。

turns.en: No, we don't know. Do you have a list of like, here are some cool locations, let's see if we can get them and then like often get told no? Absolutely. If you want to like get the intrepid, like how easy is that? And when you call and you say, hi, we run a puzzle hunt with a lot of golden people. Like, does that work? Or people are like, what are you talking about?
turns.zh: 这个我们可就不知道了。你们会不会有一份清单，写着『这些是很酷的场地，看看能不能拿下』，然后经常被人拒绝？绝对会。如果你想拿下『无畏号』，那有多容易？你打电话过去说：『嗨，我们办一场谜题寻宝，来的都是高盛（Goldman）的人。』这招管用吗？还是对方一脸懵：『你在说什么？』

turns.en: It's everything. We didn't get the Intrepid. I think that was the year before we started working with them. So I can't speak to specifically renting the Intrepid, but it's always... Yeah, at midnight. Yeah, or into 2 a.m. Some things are, wow, we're never going to get that. And then people come back to us and like, yeah, how about $ 2, 500? And you're like, great, let's do it.
turns.zh: 什么都有可能。『无畏号』我们没拿下，我记得那是在我们接手之前一年的事。所以租用『无畏号』的具体情况我说不好，但总是……对，在午夜，或者拖到凌晨两点。有些场地你会想：哇，这个我们肯定拿不下。结果对方回头跟我们说：『嗯，2500 美元怎么样？』你就想：太好了，成交。

turns.en: What's the most surprising location or thing you've gotten access to?
turns.zh: 你们拿到过的最出人意料的场地或东西是什么？

turns.en: Last game, we did a puzzle in FAO Schwartz where teams had to play the big piano with their feet to solve a puzzle. That was a really fun one for someone who grew up watching the movie Big with Tom Hanks.
turns.zh: 上一届，我们在 FAO Schwartz 玩具店里做了一道谜题，各队必须用脚去弹那架大钢琴（big piano）来解谜。对于一个从小看着汤姆·汉克斯（Tom Hanks）那部电影《飞越未来》（Big）长大的人来说，这真的太好玩了。

turns.en: We could also ask the inverse of that question. I mean, where have you been turned down from that you really wanted to happen?
turns.zh: 我们也可以反过来问。我是说，有没有哪个你们特别想拿下、却被拒绝的地方？

turns.en: Every year there's a theme. In 2023, it was the Lost Cosmonauts, which is a riff on a conspiracy theory that there's cosmonauts that were launched into space. that we'd never heard about. And kind of the seed of the idea is that somehow they're still alive and we have to bring them home. And so we were going to do a cosmonaut training course, like in a swimming pool in New York city. And so I was trying to get, you know, one of those huge inflatable, like water obstacle courses, you know, we were going to like order this $ 10, 000 inflatable obstacle course from China and then like set it up in an Olympic size pool in New York city. And it just did not fly. And, you know, we had a, a poor Good Shepherd staffer who was in charge of trying to find me my swimming pool. And she was just like, Ryan, I don't think anyone's going to let us inflate this giant obstacle course in the pool.
turns.zh: 每年都有一个主题。2023 年的主题是『失落的宇航员』（Lost Cosmonauts），它是对一个阴谋论的改编——据说有些宇航员被送上了太空，而我们从来没听说过他们。这个点子的内核是：不知怎么的，他们还活着，我们得把他们带回家。所以我们本来打算做一个『宇航员训练课程』，就在纽约市的一个游泳池里。于是我一直在想办法弄到那种巨大的充气水上障碍赛道——我们打算从中国订一套价值 1 万美元的充气障碍赛道，然后架到纽约市一个奥林匹克标准泳池里。结果这根本行不通。你知道，我们有一位可怜的 Good Shepherd 员工，负责帮我找游泳池，她直接跟我说：『Ryan，我觉得没人会让我们在泳池里充起这么一个巨型障碍赛道的。』

turns.en: I've always wanted to do a puzzle in the Natural History Museum, like with the big whale.
turns.zh: 我一直想在自然历史博物馆（Natural History Museum）里做一道谜题，就是有大鲸鱼模型的那个。

turns.en: Night at the museum style.
turns.zh: 《博物馆奇妙夜》（Night at the Museum）那种风格。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. You have to become like an official partner of the museum. And it's like a an annual membership that costs $ 30, 000. And then there's all these other hoops you have to jump through.
turns.zh: 对，正是。你得先成为博物馆的正式合作伙伴，那是一份年费 3 万美元的会员资格，然后还有一大堆其他的关卡要你闯。

turns.en: You can get a Bloomberg terminal with that. Jeez.
turns.zh: 这钱都够买一台彭博终端（Bloomberg terminal）了。天呐。

turns.en: Some of the best locations we've had are like the rooftop of the Port Authority bus terminal. On the north end of the Port Authority bus terminal, there's an uncovered parking deck that anyone can access. And you can look down 41st Street all the way to the library, through Times Square, through Bryant Park. And at night, it's one of the most... incredible places in New York City. And it's just sitting there for anyone to come and see, or we'll like park a box truck on the side of the street and have people go in. And there's like a speakeasy type establishment with like a live band inside a box truck delivery truck just parked on the side of the road. And so the venues that we love are those types of unexpected delight that kind of like are hidden in that New York City is so good at kind of concealing.
turns.zh: 我们用过的最棒的场地之一，是港务局客运总站（Port Authority bus terminal）的天台。在港务局客运总站的北端，有一个任何人都能上去的露天停车层。你可以顺着 41 街一路望到图书馆，穿过时代广场（Times Square）、穿过布莱恩特公园（Bryant Park）。到了夜里，那是纽约市最……令人难以置信的地方之一。它就在那儿，等着任何人来看。或者我们会把一辆厢式货车停在路边，让人进去——里面就像一个『地下酒吧』（speakeasy）式的场所，还有一支现场乐队，全都装在一辆停在路边的厢式送货卡车里。所以我们钟爱的场地，正是那种『意想不到的惊喜』，它们藏匿在纽约特别擅长隐藏的角落里。

turns.en: What about like best puzzles, right? So you've talked about like The simplest level is like you get handed a piece of paper and you do some piece of paper. Like certainly like at Midnight Madness with production values, what they are like, there are some amount of like doing puzzles on cool physical objects. Like what are some like cool physical objects that have been purposed as puzzles?
turns.zh: 那最好的谜题呢？你们说到最简单的层次就是：有人递给你一张纸，你就着这张纸做点文章。但在 Midnight Madness 这种制作水准下，肯定有相当一部分是在酷炫的实体物件上解谜。有哪些被用作谜题的酷炫实体物件？

turns.en: I have one sitting right here. It's like a Palantir orb crystal ball that we distributed.
turns.zh: 我这儿就摆着一个。它像一个 Palantir 水晶球（orb），是我们分发出去的。

turns.en: You're holding up a crystal ball.
turns.zh: 你正举着一个水晶球。

turns.en: Yeah, holding up a crystal ball. And it reacts with different colors and flashing patterns based on where you are geographically. And so there was a whole puzzle in 2021 scattered all over Central Park. And as you approach different locations, the globe did different things and flash different color sequences. And then those were decoded. One of my favorite puzzles from, I think this is an Alicia, I don't know, but I've read about it in one of the many articles that I'm sure you guys said was the circuit board where you had to assemble a circuit board and then one of the transistors overheated and you discovered that the circuit board was actually a, a map of New York City subway stations. And when you looked at it through a infrared camera, you know, it was identifying which station to go to. So that's another example of something that lives in my head as a great use of a physical object.
turns.zh: 对，举着一个水晶球。它会根据你所处的地理位置，用不同的颜色和闪烁模式做出反应。2021 年有一整套谜题散布在整个中央公园（Central Park）里，当你走近不同地点时，这个球就会做出不同的动作、闪出不同的颜色序列，然后这些序列会被解码。我最喜欢的谜题之一——我想这是 Alicia 设计的，我也说不准，但我在你们提到过的众多文章里读到过——是那道电路板（circuit board）谜题：你得组装一块电路板，然后其中一个晶体管过热，你由此发现这块电路板其实是纽约市地铁站的一张地图。当你透过红外相机（infrared camera）去看它时，它就会指出该去哪个地铁站。所以这是另一个例子，在我脑海里算是把实体物件用得极妙的典范。

turns.en: Just to go back to Midnight Madness really quickly.
turns.zh: 我快速回到 Midnight Madness 这个话题。

turns.en: I mean, so you have.
turns.zh: 我是说，你们有……

turns.en: These three to four to five hour puzzles, I believe you said. Midnight Madness seems like a different beast entirely in that, you know, it runs overnight.
turns.zh: 这些三到四到五个小时的谜题，我记得你们是这么说的。而 Midnight Madness 似乎完全是另一种物种，因为它通宵进行。

turns.en: Yeah, like what is your time expectation for this year's Midnight Madness? Like when does it start and when do you expect the last team to finish?
turns.zh: 是啊，那今年这场 Midnight Madness，你们的时间预期是怎样的？几点开始，你们预计最后一支队伍几点结束？

turns.en: Yeah, about 12 to 14 hours, depending on how fast teams are. The idea is to start it early afternoon, one or two, and then it ends sometime shortly after midnight. Hopefully not too much longer than that.
turns.zh: 大概 12 到 14 个小时，取决于各队有多快。设想是午后一两点开始，然后在午夜过后不久结束。希望别拖太久。

turns.en: So it's in early October. When do you start planning for it?
turns.zh: 所以是在十月初。你们什么时候开始筹备？

turns.en: Typically about a year in advance. So it's about a year in the making.
turns.zh: 通常提前大约一年。所以整个制作周期大概是一年。

turns.en: Do you design games for a lot of big Wall Street? Can you say your repeat clients or something?
turns.zh: 你们为很多华尔街大机构设计游戏吗？能说说你们的回头客户之类的吗？

turns.en: Yes, we have a lot of Wall Street clients. That's our biggest audience and our biggest client base.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有很多华尔街客户。那是我们最大的受众、也是最大的客户群。

turns.en: We have like NDAs.
turns.zh: 我们签了保密协议（NDA）。

turns.en: In your business, you do like relatively short, like one day events for like team building events for companies who hire you to design games, right? Yeah.
turns.zh: 在你们的业务里，你们会为那些雇你们设计游戏的公司做那种相对短、比如一天的团建活动，对吧？嗯。

turns.en: Three to four hours long based on how much we think that they can take or how much we know that they can take. As we have repeat clients, we start to understand the culture of the company and what they're looking for and what they can handle. And yeah, there's been some.
turns.zh: 时长三到四个小时，取决于我们觉得他们能承受多少、或者我们知道他们能承受多少。随着有了回头客户，我们开始了解这家公司的文化、他们想要什么、以及他们扛得住什么。是的，其中有些……

turns.en: Who can handle the most?
turns.zh: 谁最能扛？

turns.en: Well, you know, there's a difference between who can handle the most and who wants to give off the vibe like they can handle the most. We can answer both. We have NDA. All of these companies are so secretive.
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道，『谁最能扛』和『谁想营造出自己能扛的范儿』是两码事。这两个我们都能回答。我们签了保密协议。这些公司都太神秘了。

turns.en: We'll bleep them out.
turns.zh: 我们会把名字消音的。

turns.en: It's really hard. Fortunately, Bridgewater has been very generous that they allow us to talk to say that we have done many hunts for them. And they actually came to us only recently in 2021 after they did Midnight Madness, formerly known as Compass, with us. And we've worked with them multiple times a year for different teams. And they're awesome to work with.
turns.zh: 这真的很难。好在桥水（Bridgewater）很大方，允许我们对外说，我们为他们做过很多场寻宝。其实他们是最近才找上我们的——2021 年，在跟我们一起玩过 Midnight Madness（前身叫 Compass）之后。此后我们一年为他们不同的团队做好几次。跟他们合作非常愉快。

turns.en: I do want to know where Bridgewater falls on the can't handle things and want to give the impression, but it seems rude to make you answer.
turns.zh: 我确实想知道，桥水是落在『扛不住』那一档，还是『想营造能扛的印象』那一档，但逼你们回答好像不太礼貌。

turns.en: They're great. I mean, don't make us pick between our children. We love all of our puzzle children equally. And the only thing I'll say is specifically the team we work for does love the puzzly puzzles. You know, there's definitely a gradient of people that love the experience, they love the locations and the feedback we get from Bridgewater, at least the point of contact who helps us plan their events is that they want the puzzles, they want the goods.
turns.zh: 他们很棒。我是说，别让我们在自家孩子里挑。我们平等地爱我们所有的『谜题孩子』。我唯一会说的是：具体到我们对接的那个团队，他们是真爱那种『硬核谜题』。你知道，人群里肯定有个梯度：有人爱的是体验、爱的是场地；而我们从桥水那里得到的反馈——至少从帮我们策划活动的那位对接人那里——是他们要的是谜题，要的是真家伙。

turns.en: Yeah, they want the brutality. They like it to be difficult.
turns.zh: 对，他们要那种残酷劲儿，喜欢它有难度。

turns.en: And it's been really interesting for us as, again, outsiders, like we both went to art school, figuring out what's the difference between like a Quant hedge fund and a Bridgewater and a Goldman and where they all function in this world. It's been quite the education.
turns.zh: 对我们这两个『局外人』来说——我俩都是艺术院校出身的——去搞清楚量化对冲基金、桥水、高盛之间到底有什么区别、它们各自在这个世界里扮演什么角色，真的很有意思。这着实是一堂大开眼界的课。

turns.en: They each have a different culture that manifests differently in our games. And often the culture is kind of inspired by the founder.
turns.zh: 它们各有各的文化，在我们的游戏里表现出不同的样子。而这种文化往往是受创始人影响形成的。

turns.en: Like some of.
turns.zh: 比如其中有些……

turns.en: Them are work hard, play hard, and they like to party hard. And that's a culture that emanates from the founder. And some of them are more like about work-life balance and generosity. And they each kind of have a very distinct culture that we can recognize just in our limited touch points through our games. And also when a lot of our client base was more tech, like Google and Meta and tech firms, we joke about like making our own private investments based on how well we see people doing in our games. Because we definitely recognize that companies that are doing well for us were also doing well in the market.
turns.zh: ……是『努力工作、尽情玩乐』型的，喜欢往死里狂欢，而这种文化正是从创始人身上散发出来的。还有一些更讲究工作与生活的平衡、更慷慨大方。它们各自都有非常鲜明的文化，哪怕只是通过我们游戏里那有限的几个接触点，我们也能识别出来。另外，当我们的客户群更多是科技公司时——比如谷歌（Google）、Meta 这些科技公司——我们会开玩笑说，可以根据大家在游戏里的表现来决定我们自己私下投什么。因为我们确实注意到：那些在我们游戏里表现好的公司，在市场上也表现好。

turns.en: And then when those same companies three years later stopped doing well, it meant something.
turns.zh: 而三年后，当这些同样的公司不再表现好时，那也是有意义的。

turns.en: Hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Stop doing around the puzzles. The puzzles were like a leading indicator of the stock or. Exactly. Yeah. Has a hedge fund ever been like, you're good at puzzles. Come work for us.
turns.zh: （在谜题上）也不再表现好了。这些谜题就像是股票的领先指标，或者说……没错。是啊。有没有哪家对冲基金说过：『你很擅长解谜题，来给我们干活吧。』

turns.en: Not in-house, but we know some hedge funds that do have in-house puzzle creators and have hired our friends as in-house puzzle creators. So it exists. It's a thing.
turns.zh: 没有（找我们）做内部的，但我们知道有些对冲基金确实养着内部的谜题设计者，还雇了我们的朋友去做内部谜题设计。所以这是存在的，是个真实的行当。

turns.en: I've seen some of that.
turns.zh: 我也见过一些这样的情况。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Because like, clearly, like there is a big, like recruiting dynamic of a lot of these firms like to hire people who are good at puzzles. They like to pose puzzles to them as part of the recruiting process. They like to attract people who like puzzles. So that seemed like an overlap. In the puzzle creator community, is there like a trend where a lot of people have a certain degree or a certain background?
turns.zh: 因为显然，这里面有一个很大的招聘逻辑：很多这类公司喜欢雇擅长解谜题的人。他们喜欢在招聘过程中给候选人出谜题，喜欢吸引那些爱好谜题的人。所以这看起来是一处重合。那么在谜题设计者这个圈子里，是不是有一种趋势——很多人都有某种学位或某种背景？

turns.en: Certainly, yeah. Stats, math, business, definitely. But then there's also people who do a lot of more linguistic puzzles. There's like a whole kind of like the crossword, you know, that whole world is a little more linguistic and they have a different background.
turns.zh: 当然，是的。统计、数学、商科，绝对有。但也有很多人做的是更偏语言类的谜题。就像填字游戏（crossword）那一整个世界，更偏语言一些，他们的背景也不一样。

turns.en: When I've done puzzle hunts, there's always a cryptic crossword cluing type puzzle, and I'm always the guy who solves those. That's my one contribution to the team.
turns.zh: 我玩谜题寻宝时，总会有一道那种『隐语填字』（cryptic crossword）式的谜题，而我永远是解出那类题的人。这是我对队伍唯一的贡献。

turns.en: Right, right.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: A good puzzle creation team has... A good puzzle is created by people with a lot of different backgrounds.
turns.zh: 一支好的谜题设计团队会有……一道好谜题，是由背景各异的一群人来打造的。

turns.en: I assume that when you do team building events, it's a company for 200 people, but do you ever have these five people who are going to do a puzzle hunt together?
turns.zh: 我猜你们做团建活动时，通常是一家两百人的公司，但你们有没有接过那种就五个人、要一起去做一场谜题寻宝的？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 有。

turns.en: I mean, yeah. If you can afford us, we'll do it. And we've done... groups as small as four and groups as large as, what, 300, 400, John?
turns.zh: 我是说，有啊。只要你出得起钱，我们就做。我们接过的团队小至四人，大至……多少来着，300、400 人吧，John？

turns.en: Wait, can you tell me about the groups of four? Like, how does that come in?
turns.zh: 等等，能说说四人团吗？这种是怎么来的？

turns.en: Either someone's birthday. It's a birthday party, usually.
turns.zh: 要么是某个人的生日。通常是生日派对。

turns.en: It's like someone who really likes puzzles.
turns.zh: 就是那种特别喜欢谜题的人。

turns.en: Someone who really likes puzzles. And either they can afford our services because we just run a past event for them, or they have a ton of money and we do something completely tailored to them that's like, all about their life and all about their 50 years and all about their kids. And those are really fun too.
turns.zh: 就是特别喜欢谜题的人。要么他们付得起我们的服务，我们就把过去办过的某场活动直接给他们跑一遍；要么他们有的是钱，我们就为他们完全量身定制一场——全是围绕他们的人生、他们的五十岁、他们的孩子来设计的。那种也非常好玩。

turns.en: We've done many birthdays for CEOs of like hedge funds.
turns.zh: 我们给不少对冲基金的 CEO 办过生日。

turns.en: Yeah, I was going to say like, this feels like a classic hedge fund manager 50th birthday party.
turns.zh: 是啊，我正想说，这感觉就是典型的对冲基金经理五十岁生日派对。

turns.en: We did one hedge fund who said that they wanted, maybe if you want to talk about our white whale was the one of the co-CEOs of this is a small fund. And they said, okay, I'm going to, I want to do this across Europe for my 50th birthday. And I was like, yes, let's do it. Call us. And then they never showed.
turns.zh: 有一家对冲基金说他们想……如果要聊我们的『白鲸』（white whale，指可遇不可求的大单），那是一家小型基金的联席 CEO。他说：『好，我要为我的五十岁生日把这场活动办遍整个欧洲。』我心想：太好了，来办吧，联系我们。结果他们再也没出现。

turns.en: But did you have a preliminary budget?
turns.zh: 但你们当时有初步预算吗？

turns.en: No, no, we didn't. We didn't even get that far. But it was it was a really it was for a fund that was celebrating their 25th anniversary, I think, in London. And so we got to build a six hour hunt in London. And that was one of our favorites, still our favorite jobs to date. But It could have been the lead-in to a cross-Europe scavenger hunt, but it wasn't to be.
turns.zh: 没有没有，我们没有，连那一步都没走到。但那是为一家基金做的，我记得是他们在伦敦庆祝成立 25 周年。所以我们得以在伦敦搭建一场六小时的寻宝。那是我们的最爱之一，至今仍是我最喜欢的项目。它本可以成为一场『横跨欧洲寻物游戏』的引子，但终究没能成行。

turns.en: Yeah. Wait, you said something about you had a lot of tech clients and now you have fewer tech clients and it's more finance-gearing? What do you think is causing that?
turns.zh: 嗯。等等，你们刚说以前有很多科技客户，现在科技客户变少了、更多转向金融了？你们觉得是什么造成的？

turns.en: Yeah, we've definitely seen the shift from when tech was the coolest place to be and now these companies have matured and they're still great places to work, but there's a little less of an edge to them. I think we've seen... they're also working a little less hard at employer retention and they're pulling back the perks. And so we've seen pre-pandemic specifically, we do a lot of like 50 to 80% events for big tech companies, growing tech companies, that sort of thing. And then post-pandemic, we've seen a lot fewer tech companies. And when the tech companies do come, this is more of a return to office thing, but it's a much smaller group. So people are getting together in much smaller groups, they're going out with their, their immediate five to 12 team members and not their full division or whatever. And so we, at the same time, we've seen a lot more hedge funds and AI companies coming in. And so, yeah, as the type of company where young, ambitious, really smart people work at kind of shifts, we do see that in our, in our clients as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们确实看到了这种转变：从科技业还是『最酷去处』的时候，到现在这些公司成熟了——它们依然是很棒的工作场所，但那股锋芒少了一点。我们看到……它们在『留住员工』这件事上也没那么卖力了，福利也在往回收。具体来说，疫情前，我们 50% 到 80% 的活动都是为大型科技公司、成长中的科技公司这类的做的。疫情后，科技公司少了很多。而当科技公司真的来了，这更多是一种『回归办公室』（return to office）的活动，但规模小得多。所以大家是以更小的群体聚会，只跟自己身边那五到十二个团队成员出去，而不是整个部门。与此同时，我们看到更多的对冲基金和 AI 公司找上门来。所以，是啊，随着那种『年轻、有野心、极聪明的人去哪儿工作』的风向转变，我们在自己的客户结构里也看到了这种变化。

turns.en: So it's like, if you work at Facebook, like 10 years ago, you were like, Oh, I really want to solve puzzles. Like I'm motivated to like, use my brain. And now it's like, yeah, I'm going to rest and rest and not go on a puzzle hunt.
turns.zh: 所以就像是：十年前你要是在 Facebook 上班，你会想『哦，我超想解谜题，我特别有动力去动脑子』。而现在则是『行吧，我就歇着、歇着，不去玩什么谜题寻宝了』。

turns.en: I don't want to say exactly, but yeah, that's a little bit of the vibe I get. One of the reasons that I started reading money stuff was after you wrote that huge crypto article, Matt. And at the same time, we were building a completely bespoke kind of alternate reality game puzzle community for a NFT firm. And we had no idea what we were doing in crypto, no idea what we were doing with NFTs. And so Reading your article helped me like get my head around this whole concept as we were building out this game, community, world, IP universe that we were hired to do kind of like as an extension of the Bored Ape Yacht Club universe. And it was- Did you get paid? We did get paid.
turns.zh: 我不想说得太绝对，但是啊，那确实是我感受到的一点氛围。我开始读《Money Stuff》的原因之一，就是在你写了那篇关于加密货币（crypto）的长文之后，Matt。而与此同时，我们正在为一家 NFT 公司打造一个完全定制的『平行现实游戏』（alternate reality game）谜题社群。我们当时对加密货币一窍不通，对 NFT 也一无所知。所以读你的文章帮我理清了整个概念，而那正是我们在搭建这个游戏、社群、世界、IP 宇宙的时候——我们受雇把它打造成『无聊猿游艇俱乐部』（Bored Ape Yacht Club）宇宙的一个延伸。当时是——你们拿到钱了吗？我们确实拿到了钱。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah, we got paid. It was an incredible, incredible experience. And we got to create characters and create stories. And sometimes our events are a little more puzzle-y oriented. And this was the most built out we've ever created a whole world. We created locations and characters and plot points and betrayals and stashed puzzles in lockers at the LAX airport and in bars in London and slipped burner phones. And it was a really fun event. Now, the project as a whole didn't survive more than a few years, but we kind of were in this at one of the, the crypto bull markets. And, uh, that's a real moment in time.
turns.zh: 是的，我们拿到钱了。那是一次难以置信、难以置信的经历。我们得以创造角色、创造故事。有时候我们的活动会更偏谜题一点，而这一次是我们有史以来最完整地搭建出的一整个世界。我们创造了地点、角色、情节点、背叛，把谜题藏在洛杉矶国际机场（LAX）的储物柜里、藏在伦敦的酒吧里，还偷偷塞进一次性『燃烧手机』（burner phones）。那真是一场非常好玩的活动。当然，这个项目整体没能撑过几年，但我们算是赶上了加密货币的一波牛市参与其中。呃，那真是一个特定时刻的产物。

turns.en: I know we've talked about hedge funds and tech firms. Like we didn't even talk about like, what does the chart of like your crypto exposure look like?
turns.zh: 我知道我们聊了对冲基金和科技公司。但我们甚至还没聊到——你们加密货币业务敞口的那张曲线图长什么样？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: It was all crypto firms and then you never heard from them again.
turns.zh: 一度全是加密公司，然后你就再也没他们的消息了。

turns.en: It's that's pretty much it.
turns.zh: 差不多就是这样。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: We haven't done any of our private kind of team building events for crypto firms. This was a, kind of like a public-facing event for the crypto community. And it was led by a guy who wanted to create this series of IP around some of the Bored Apes, or to be more specific, the Mutant Apes, which is a whole sub-genre of apes.
turns.zh: 我们没为加密公司做过任何那种私密的团建活动。这一次算是面向公众、为加密社群办的活动。它由一个人牵头，他想围绕其中一些『无聊猿』（Bored Apes）——更准确说是『变异猿』（Mutant Apes），那是猿猴里的一个完整子门类——打造一系列 IP。

turns.en: And I think we'll end it there.
turns.zh: 我想我们就聊到这儿吧。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 好好好，正是。

turns.en: John and Ryan, thank you so much for coming on. This was fun.
turns.zh: John 和 Ryan，非常感谢你们来做客，这很有趣。

turns.en: Thank you for having us.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我们。

turns.en: It's great to be here. Hope to see you on the streets.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。希望在街头见到你们。

turns.en: Thank you, guys.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们，各位。

turns.en: Honored to be your sanctuary guests.
turns.zh: 很荣幸成为你们的座上宾。

turns.en: Yeah, wow, what a distinction. And that was the Money Stuff podcast. I'm Matt Levine.
turns.zh: 是啊，哇，这称呼可真特别。以上就是《Money Stuff》播客。我是 Matt Levine。

turns.en: And I'm Katie Greifeld.
turns.zh: 我是 Katie Greifeld。

turns.zh: 你可以在 Bloomberg.com 上订阅《Money Stuff》通讯（newsletter）来阅读我的作品。

turns.zh: 你也可以每天在彭博电视台（Bloomberg TV）的《Open Interest》节目里看到我，美东时间上午 9 点到 11 点。

turns.zh: 我们很乐意收到你们的来信。你可以发邮件到 moneypod@Bloomberg.net，向我们提个问题，我们也许会在节目里回答。
